summary_text: Haier Showcases ... AI-Powered Smart ... Systems at IFA 2026 ... Haier's IFA 2026 press release claims AI-powered washers, fridges, ovens and TVs that sense, learn and adapt. For AI practitioners, the key questions are architecture, inference location and whether the computer vision works reliably outside demo conditions. 6h ago · 4 min read · Verified by 2 sources · By AI Intelligence Brief ... 1. 1 Haier's September 6, 2026 press release announced an AI-powered smart home ecosystem spanning garment care, refrigeration, cooking, entertainment, digital services and robotics at IFA 2026. 2. 2 The Vision 15 washing machine uses an internal camera, sensors and algorithms to detect load size, balance and foam levels, then adjusts water levels, detergent dosing, drum movement and program settings. 3. 3 The Maestro refrigerator prototype features AI Food Care System 2.0, which recognizes stored ingredients and recommends suitable storage conditions. 4. 4 The ID Ultimate Series 6 oven uses an internal camera to recognize food, monitor cooking progress and stop the program when the desired result is reached. 5. 5 UltraSense AI analyzes content and ambient conditions to adjust picture and sound on Haier Smart TVs in real time. 6. 6 The hOn app brings Haier Europe's connected products, services and home experiences together in a single digital environment. ... Global home appliance and consumer electronics company; claims No.1 in major home appliances for 17 consecutive years per Euromonitor. ... ## Analysis Beyond the consumer marketing, Haier's IFA 2026 announcement is a signal that edge AI, computer vision and sensor fusion are moving into mass-market home appliances. The Vision 15 washer, Maestro fridge, ID Ultimate Series 6 oven and UltraSense AI TV each claim real-time perception and adaptive control, but the release avoids architecture details. AI builders should watch whether this is genuine on-device inference or cloud-dependent demo logic. At IFA 2026 in Berlin, Haier used a press release distributed on September 6 to announce an AI-powered smart home ecosystem that spans garment care, refrigeration, cooking, entertainment, digital services and robotics. The company, which says Euromonitor International has ranked it the world's No. 1 brand in major home appliances for 17 consecutive years, presented the showcase under the theme "Home of Intelligent Possibilities." Because the only available sources are press releases, the following details represent Haier's own claims rather than independently verified reporting. The announcement describes a progression from individual connected appliances to a coordinated home that senses conditions, understands context, learns from user habits and adapts device operation. > “ > > The Vision 15 washer, Maestro fridge, ID Ultimate Series 6 oven and UltraSense AI TV each claim real-time perception and adaptive control, but the release avoids architecture details. The most concrete technical claim centers on the Vision 15 washing machine. According to Haier, the machine uses an internal camera, sensors and algorithms to detect factors such as load size, balance and foam levels, then adjusts water levels, detergent dosing, drum movement and program settings. That description implies real-time sensor fusion and on-device or hybrid edge inference, though Haier does not disclose the underlying architecture. For AI practitioners, the interesting question is whether these adjustments happen locally, in the cloud, or through a combination of both, and whether the system's learning is personalized per household or based on fleet-level models. In refrigeration, Haier presented the Maestro prototype, which brings together preservation technologies under its AI Food Care System 2.0. The company claims the system recognizes stored ingredients and recommends suitable conditions to help users manage food more effectively. This is computer vision applied to a use case with significant commercial potential: reducing food waste and improving freshness. The oven category follows the same pattern. The ID Ultimate Series 6 oven uses an internal camera to recognize food, monitor cooking progress and stop the program when the desired result has been reached. This kind of closed-loop sensing and actuation is a notable step beyond timer-based cooking, though the release does not specify which food types or cooking outcomes the system can reliably detect. In the living room, UltraSense AI analyzes content and ambient conditions to adjust picture and sound on Haier Smart TVs in real time. The hOn app ties these categories together, connecting Haier Europe's products, services and home experiences in a single digital environment. The stated goal is to translate connected technology into practical benefits around daily routines, from laundry and food care to cooking and entertainment. The release claims this progression from individual products to coordinated home scenarios is already reaching users at scale, but it does not provide metrics on active users, app engagement or the number of AI-enabled devices sold. ... ## What to Watch The announcement should be read in the context of a broader smart home market that is becoming crowded with AI claims from Samsung, LG, Bosch, Midea and others. At the same IFA event, manufacturers routinely demonstrate appliance intelligence ranging from simple machine learning to generative assistants. Haier's differentiation, as presented, is less about a single headline feature and more about coordinating multiple appliance categories through one app and shared AI logic. If the systems work as described, the strategic implication is that appliance makers can move up the value chain from hardware to software-enabled services, creating potential recurring revenue through subscriptions, insights and maintenance. However, several open questions remain. The release does not state when or where the Vision 15, ID Ultimate Series 6 or hOn features will be commercially available, and the Maestro is explicitly described as a prototype. Data privacy, reliability of computer vision in real-world kitchens and laundries, and interoperability with other ecosystems are also unaddressed. For investors in Haier Smart Home, whose Shanghai-listed shares trade under ticker 600690.SS, the IFA showcase may support the company's technology narrative, but promotional claims should not be confused with verified product performance. The forward-looking insight is that AI-powered appliances are moving from isolated features to coordinated home scenarios, and the companies that can demonstrate dependable, privacy-sensitive edge AI will be best positioned as the smart home evolves.

headline: Haier’s smart home thinks, learns and acts. Even with robots - Il Sole 24 ORE
summary_text: BERLIN – Once again, the IFA trade fair provides Haier with the perfect opportunity to reaffirm two of its key strengths: its status as a leading player in the consumer electronics sector and its strong focus on sponsoring major sporting events to boost its brand visibility. In Berlin, the Chinese firm has been confirmed as the world leader in the large white goods sector for the 17th consecutive year and has announced an agreement signed with UEFA and the European Football Clubs Association to become, from 2027 (and for the next four years) a Global Partner of the UEFA Champions League. Significant focus is therefore placed on the brand, but also on a vision of the smart home that goes beyond simply adding a new smart function to a household appliance. The new frontier is ensuring that the home learns to understand what is happening within it and can intervene, when necessary, without waiting for the user to issue a single command or configure a specific mode of use for the device. Haier Europe’s slogan at Messe Berlin, ‘Home of Intelligent Possibilities’, can therefore be interpreted as a transition from a merely connected home to an ecosystem capable of interpreting its context, learning from the habits of those living within it, and coordinating the products and services that characterise their daily lives. The artificial intelligence integrated into various appliances (from washing machines to televisions) functions in this regard as a cross-cutting infrastructure spanning research and development, design (based on consumer scenarios and needs), production, user experience and after-sales services. The ultimate goal? To make technology increasingly invisible and capable of adapting to real-life situations, whilst leaving control in the hands of the user. ... In the new product announcements made in Berlin, the concepts of ‘new intelligence’ are being put into practice across all segments. In the washing cycle, for example, the Vision 15 uses a camera built into the washing machine door to monitor the load and recognise the quantity of laundry, colours, suds and any items that may have been left in the drum. Sensors and algorithms (AI Power Sense and AI Vision Sense) detect, interpret and process information relating to weight, balance, water level and temperature to automatically set various cycle parameters. As Haier’s managers explain, this technological innovation therefore operates ‘behind the scenes’, and the same applies to kitchen appliances. The AI Food Care System integrated into fridges is able to recognise food and suggest how to store it; the AI Vision system fitted to the ID Ultimate Series 6 ovens does the same with food to monitor the entire cooking cycle, automatically stopping the programme when the set result is achieved. Induction hobs and cooker hoods are also becoming increasingly intelligent: the former can transfer a pan’s cooking settings when it is moved (by detecting its position), whilst the latter can be activated simply with a gesture thanks to the MotionSense function. The digital backbone of the entire ecosystem is hOn, the app-based platform through which Haier manages products and services remotely within a single environment to intelligently optimise energy consumption. In this regard, as explained by Haier Europe’s CEO, Neil Tunstall, the Chinese company is set to invest 13 billion euros over the next five years in AI and IoT technologies, with the aim of bringing distributed intelligence into homes and introducing appliances capable not only of seeing, recognising and making decisions, but also of interacting with machines (robots) capable of physically acting within the home environment. ... Whilst the Vision 15 range of washing machines represents the pinnacle of Haier’s technology in the field of laundry, the most ‘eye-catching’ new product showcased at IFA is the Multi Care Collection, a range of appliances designed to meet the need to run cycles with different loads simultaneously, thereby increasing flexibility in the home. The Multi Care Laundry Studio is, in fact, a product featuring four independent drums – one for the 10 kg washing machine, two 1 kg drums and one for the 8 kg tumble dryer – allowing each compartment to be managed separately, so that items differing in quantity, fabric or colour can be washed together. In the refrigeration sector, the Horizon Collection brings AI to the day-to-day management of food: the Hydro Hub model incorporates food and drink recognition, whilst the Maestro prototype brings together advanced proprietary preservation technologies – such as the AI Defrost Zone, designed to defrost food whilst minimising moisture loss and preserving quality – within a single system. The new I-Pro Shine A-70%, for its part, applies the same philosophy to dishwashers, using sensors and algorithms to adjust water, temperature, cycle time and energy consumption according to the load. For those with an eye for aesthetics, this functional dimension, enhanced by AI capabilities, takes shape in the Aura Collection: the various appliances (oven, microwave, hob, cooker hood and dishwasher) share the same design language and are distinguished by ‘Aura Grey’, a fingerprint-resistant finish applied to the glass that changes appearance depending on the light and surroundings. ... . AI Sound, on the other hand, works on voice separation, frequency balancing and volume to make dialogue clearer and the soundscape more uniform (on some models, the audio is handled by Sound by KEF, the historic British brand). For those using the television with a games console or a PC, AI Game works to reduce input lag, screen tearing and interruptions. Finally, AI Eye Caring adjusts brightness and contrast to suit ambient lighting conditions and the content to enhance viewing comfort. The range features various panel technologies, from QD-Mini LED to OLED, with screen sizes up to 115 inches. Whilst the spectacular innovation showcased at IFA is an impressive 163-inch Micro LED screen (created by combining multiple panels), the manufacturer’s decision to pair LED backlighting with technologies such as the Pure RGB Light Engine (in the new MR92 series from 55 inches upwards) and Super Quantum Dot Colour (on the new MS 96 range from 100 inches) – which work on the ... The real big news (in terms of future prospects) that the Chinese company unveiled at IFA comes, however, from the field of robotics, The humanoid robots on display at Haier’s stand – capable of perceiving their surroundings and acting within them, interacting with people and household appliances – are perhaps the most striking expression of the ‘Home of Intelligent Possibilities’ vision. We’re talking about systems that load and unload the washing and organise food in the fridge, which recognise and categorise items to be cleaned, distinguishing between different types of dirt and deciding what action to take. These are companion robots that provide personal assistance through voice interaction (in Italia, a connection with smartwatches is currently being developed) in everyday activities. Intelligence is therefore not confined to software but takes shape in a physical body (‘embodied intelligence’), such as that of the W3 Exoskeleton, a carbon and titanium alloy exoskeleton that uses sensors and AI algorithms to reduce physical effort, interpreting the wearer’s movement intentions in real time and automatically adjusting the level of assistance based on their characteristics and the activity being performed. headline: Packaging industry turns to data and technology for EPR compliance
summary_text: - Global EPR requirements are pushing packaging companies to adopt more data-driven systems for regulatory reporting, traceability, and transparency. - Recyda and Constantia Flexibles highlight unified packaging data, automated calculations, and design-stage forecasting as key tools for managing compliance risks and eco-modulated fees. - Flint Group is developing deinkable, low-migration, and traceability-supporting ink technologies as recyclability, chemical safety, and food-contact rules tighten. ... Flint Group, a provider of inks and coatings, tailored solutions, digital print consumables, and digital engines for the packaging industry, tells us how technological developments in the ink sector can support compliance with emerging EPRs. ... “Technology is fundamental to translating regulatory requirements into practical, effective solutions, and we work tirelessly to upgrade our ink portfolio by implementing new technologies across our product line,” says Sarah Young, global regulatory affairs director at Flint Group. “A key focus for us is developing ink systems tailored for specific regulatory requirements, such as optimized migration inks for food contact packaging and deinkable solutions that support recycling processes.” ... Flint Group is seeing a growing interest from customers in technologies that support traceability and waste management. “For example, digital watermarking, high-resolution QR codes, and special effect inks. These solutions support improved sorting and identification within recycling streams and help to improve overall quality control and supply chain transparency,” Young adds. ... “The pace of regulatory change is increasing, particularly around sustainability, chemical safety, and food contact compliance, and that is directly guiding development of our ink systems. We are seeing increased demand for solutions that actively enable recyclability, not least of which are deinkable systems that support material recovery.” ... Bio-based and lower-impact raw materials are becoming more prevalent in ink formulations as manufacturers seek solutions to lower their carbon footprint, according to the ink company. “At the same time, tightening restrictions on chemical substances are encouraging reformulation to remove or replace materials that no longer meet regulatory acceptance. Migration performance for food contact packaging is an area where expectations are tightening particularly quickly, resulting in a need for more precise formulation and robust testing protocols.” ... In response to these changes, Flint Group Packaging Solutions has committed to embedding compliance into product design from the outset rather than treating it as a downstream requirement, Young states. “We also proactively collaborate with industry associations, regulatory bodies, and our customers to better anticipate change and translate requirements as they evolve into practical, scalable ink technologies that support greater compliance.” ... Flint Group says it develops ink systems tailored for specific regulatory requirements. Flint Group further outlines that the overall direction for packaging regulations is trending toward stricter requirements and a broader scope. “We are often seeing customers looking for solutions that can work across multiple markets.” ... “However, such solutions are difficult to find when regulations continue to vary by region in terms of how materials are defined and restricted,” Young continues. At the same time, the number of approved raw materials is gradually decreasing as more substances come under review, she adds. “This trend is resulting in fewer available chemical tools for ink formulators to meet technical demands for effective packaging solutions. Continued innovation will be required to develop alternatives that offer high technical performance while aligning with regulatory expectations.” ... Looking ahead, Young says that closer collaboration between industry and regulators will be essential to continue supporting consistency and clarity. For the ink company, this means continuing to invest in regulatory expertise and innovation, ensuring that it can anticipate change and help to guide practical pathways forward for the packaging industry. “We treat regulation as a launchpad for innovation rather than a barrier. Regulatory change may introduce complexity, but it can also provide a starting point for advancing ink technology and strengthening collaboration across the value chain,” she indicates. ... “Our regulatory and R&D teams work in close partnership to ensure that new solutions meet current requirements while also being resilient to upcoming changes.”

headline: Hidden AI SaaS: Zeta & Samsara Ride 30% Earnings Wave | SaaS Intelligence Brief
summary_text: 1. 1 LPL’s Jeff Buchbinder expects S&P 500 earnings growth could reach 30% for the current quarter, driven overwhelmingly by AI-related spending, far ahead of the 23% analyst consensus. 2. 2 Tech and AI companies are forecast to contribute 60% to 65% of total S&P 500 earnings growth, though non-tech sectors are also showing potential for 20%-plus growth. 3. 3 On June 18, Zeta Global expanded its Athena AI agent to advertising agencies, introducing agentic workflows, precision measurement, and conversational intelligence to automate marketing decisions. 4. 4 Samsara launched a disposable, paper-thin Tracking Label on June 24 that provides near-real-time shipment visibility by leveraging its network of millions of connected devices across major transit routes. 5. 5 Buchbinder cautioned that tech and semiconductor stocks look overvalued and recommended investors rotate into industrials and healthcare as second-tier AI beneficiaries. 6. 6 Insider Monkey’s list of hidden AI stocks identifies companies like Zeta Global and Samsara as overlooked plays that are embedding AI into specific verticals with potentially high recurring revenue models. ... For SaaS leaders, the AI boom isn’t just about infrastructure—it’s about embedding intelligence directly into workflows. Zeta Global’s expansion of its Athena agent and Samsara’s launch of AI-powered tracking labels demonstrate how cloud platforms are evolving from tools to autonomous decision-makers, potentially redefining recurring revenue models. The AI-fueled earnings boom is showing no signs of slowing, and market strategists are increasingly turning their attention to the lesser-known companies set to benefit from the massive capital flows into artificial intelligence. On July 2, Jeff Buchbinder, Chief Equity Strategist at LPL Financial, told BNN Bloomberg that the current earnings cycle could deliver S&P 500 growth of 30%—well above the 23% consensus—with tech and AI-related companies responsible for 60% to 65% of that expansion. While the hyperscalers and semiconductor giants capture headlines, a second layer of AI beneficiaries is quietly building robust growth narratives around specialized, vertical applications of machine learning and agentic automation. Insider Monkey’s latest screen of ‘hidden AI stocks’ spotlights precisely these under-the-radar plays, such as Zeta Global Holdings Corp. and Samsara Inc., which are embedding AI into the fabric of marketing and logistics operations, respectively. ... Zeta Global’s announcement on June 18 that it is expanding its Athena superintelligent agent to advertising agencies marks a significant step in commercializing autonomous AI workflows. Powered by its proprietary SuperGraph, which continuously ingests and analyzes consumer signals from billions of data points, Athena now offers agencies agentic workflows that monitor campaign performance autonomously, precision measurement for real-time attribution, and conversational intelligence that translates complex analytics into actionable business decisions. This move positions Zeta not merely as a marketing cloud provider but as an AI-first decisioning platform, potentially reshaping how agencies allocate billions in ad spending. The platform is currently available in beta to select partners, with a full rollout planned through the remainder of 2026, suggesting a revenue ramp that could meaningfully accelerate in the second half of the year. Samsara, a leader in connected operations, unveiled a disposable, paper-thin Tracking Label on June 24 that delivers near-real-time shipment visibility across any carrier. The label leverages the Samsara Network—a vast fabric of millions of connected devices traversing major transit routes—to offer a low-cost, scalable solution for supply chain visibility. This is a classic AI play: the label itself is a sensor, but the value lies in the AI models that interpret location data, predict delays, and optimize logistics. For Samsara, the Tracking Label expands its total addressable market beyond vehicle telematics into the high-volume parcel and freight space, potentially adding a recurring, consumption-based revenue stream that resonates with its existing SaaS model. The common thread across these picks is that they are not pure-play AI infrastructure companies but rather vertical SaaS platforms that are using AI to deepen moats, improve unit economics, and open adjacent markets. This aligns with Buchbinder’s observation that non-tech sectors and ‘second-tier AI plays’—like industrials—are also showing 20%-plus earnings growth potential. Indeed, Samsara’s roots in logistics and Zeta’s in marketing put them at the intersection of technology and traditional industry, suggesting they could attract investors seeking AI exposure without the nosebleed valuations of the Mag 7. ... ## What to Watch However, caution is warranted. Buchbinder himself noted that tech and semiconductor stocks appear ‘out over their skis’ and recommended rebalancing into healthcare and industrials. High memory prices and sticky inflation could nibble at margins, even for AI adopters. For the hidden AI cohort, the risk revolves around execution: Zeta must prove that its agentic AI can drive measurable ROI for agencies in a competitive martech landscape, while Samsara needs to demonstrate that its Tracking Label can gain adoption beyond pilot programs without cannibalizing higher-margin hardware sales. Investor sentiment could also pivot quickly if earnings fail to meet elevated expectations, making these stocks vulnerable to sharp pullbacks. Looking ahead, the AI narrative is broadening, and the companies that can embed intelligence into everyday business workflows stand to capture a disproportionate share of the value creation. As the second half of 2026 unfolds, the market will be watching to see whether these hidden AI plays can translate product momentum into the kind of earnings growth that justifies their rising valuations. For SaaS investors, the takeaway is clear: the next wave of AI value is moving from infrastructure to application, and the companies that dominate vertical SaaS with agentic capabilities could define the next growth cycle.

headline: CHEP Owner Brambles Lifts Annual Profit 4% Despite Repair Constraints -- Update | MarketScreener Hong Kong
summary_text: KT Dow Jones BRAMBLES LIMITED By Stuart Condie SYDNEY--Global pallet supplier Brambles reported a 4% rise in annual profit, meeting its downgraded guidance despite a larger-than-expected financial hit from the U.S. repair constraints that prompted a historic selloff of its stock. Australia-listed Brambles, which leases out pallets under the CHEP brand, on Thursday reported an annual underlying profit of $1.49 billion, up by 4% on the prior year once currency moves were stripped out. Sales revenue for the 12 months through June rose by 2% to $7.04 billion, also on a constant-currency basis. Brambles had initially guided for an 8% to 11% rise in underlying profit, but slashed its outlook in May to between 3% and 5% on an increase in costs from unexpected capacity constraints at subcontracted pallet service centers in parts of the U.S. The downgrade prompted the stock's largest one-day drop since 2002. Several formerly bullish analysts cut their rating and the consensus forecast for annual underlying profit fell from $1.565 billion to $1.48 billion ahead of Thursday's result announcement. Analysts had been looking for sales of $7.04 billion, according to data compiled by Visible Alpha. Brambles said its underlying profit had taken a $90 million hit from the U.S. repair constraints, exceeding its prior estimate by 50%. The effect included lost revenue and additional transport and plant costs, it said. More positively, additional fourth-quarter pallet purchases to address shortages cost $40 million, $20 million less than expected, as it utilized excess pallets in storage. Brambles, which raised its dividend to $0.2315 from $0.2083, said it expected to resolve the constraint issues by the end of December, as previously flagged. "Our actions are already delivering positive results, with customer order fulfilment improving materially since mid April," Chief Executive Graham Chipchase said. "We remain on track to resolve the repair capacity constraints by the end of the first half of FY27 and position our U.S. business to strengthen customer relationships and pursue growth." Payment for the new pallets is due in the December half and Brambles expects to spend another $60 million on an additional 2 million new pallets in the same period, resulting in a total cash outflow of $100 million. Brambles expects fiscal 2027 free cash flow before dividends of between $800 million and $950 million, down from $1.05 billion in the fiscal year just ended. It expects underlying profit growth of between 2% and 6%, and sales revenue growth of between 2% and 4%, both in constant currency terms. Brambles didn't add to the $400 million buyback extension announced in May. It expects to complete the current on-market buyback in the current fiscal year. headline: How CHEP and Animex Foods Are Jointly Shaping the Supply Chain of the Future - Logistics Monitor
summary_text: Warsaw, June 11, 2026 – In a world of growing environmental requirements and increasing pressure on supply chain efficiency, long-term partnerships are becoming strategically more important than ever. The cooperation between pallet pooling expert CHEP and meat industry leader Animex Foods demonstrates that the circular economy model can effectively support both business performance and ESG objectives. ... The cooperation between the two companies began in 2017 in response to a specific business need. As a rapidly growing organization, Animex was looking for a solution that would ensure operational stability in pallet management, reduce downtime, and streamline processes within a closed logistics structure. ... The initial pilot project quickly demonstrated that a shared-use model based on a closed-loop system—where pallets and containers are shared and reused by different manufacturers and distributors—could become much more than a sustainable operational support solution. As the owner of the pallets, CHEP was responsible for supplying, collecting, inspecting, and repairing the load carriers used by Animex Foods, allowing the customer to focus on its core business while saving both time and costs associated with pallet management. ... Over time, the cooperation expanded to additional facilities, ultimately resulting in the implementation of a consistent multi-site operating model that now supports both domestic distribution and export operations. ... Following the expansion of CHEP’s services across multiple facilities, processes and reporting were unified and standardized throughout the organization, increasing transparency and improving pallet flow management across the entire network. ... Today, the cooperation covers more than a dozen Animex Foods facilities and a significant volume of pallet movements. Its benefits are visible both operationally and financially. Reliable pallet availability, reduced shortages and downtime, and a consistent quality standard have resulted in greater predictability and efficiency throughout the supply chain. ... The partnership also involves jointly addressing challenges ranging from standardizing processes across facilities and optimizing reverse logistics flows to ensuring supply stability during periods of increased demand. Flexibility and the ability to respond quickly to changing market conditions have proven essential. ... In recent years, the cooperation between the two companies has increasingly focused on sustainability initiatives, such as developing more efficient transportation models and implementing solutions including carbon-neutral pallets. CHEP’s circular economy model supports Animex Foods in reducing CO₂ emissions and waste while also helping the company meet growing ESG reporting requirements. ... The cooperation between CHEP and Animex Foods demonstrates that a modern supply chain can be both efficient and environmentally responsible, and that well-designed logistics, built on transparency and communication, can become a genuine tool for creating competitive advantage. ... CHEP is a global leader in supply chain solutions. Working in partnership with manufacturers, retailers, and logistics providers, CHEP promotes smarter and more sustainable movement of goods in more than 60 countries worldwide. ... Through its network based on sharing, servicing, and reusing interconnected pallets, crates, and containers, CHEP helps businesses optimize their supply chains to reduce costs and minimize environmental impact. CHEP combines its leadership in the circular economy—which supports efforts to reduce emissions, waste, and single-use packaging—with a focus on resilience, helping to build future-ready supply networks through data insights, global scale, and collaboration. ... As part of the Brambles Group, CHEP manages approximately 347 million pallets and containers through a network of more than 750 service centers, employing around 11,000 people worldwide, with its largest operations in North America and Europe. ... Animex Foods is one of the largest food producers in Poland and a leader in the meat industry. The company is part of the European Morliny Foods Group, which develops its operations based on an integrated food production model and high standards of quality and safety. ... The company operates in the production and distribution of meat and processed meat products, managing a modern network of production facilities throughout Poland. It collaborates with thousands of Polish farmers, supporting the development of the domestic agri-food sector. ... Animex Foods products are distributed both on the Polish market and to customers in numerous countries across Europe and around the world. The company consistently develops its operations in line with the principles of sustainable development, focusing on efficient resource utilization, reducing environmental impact, and ensuring the highest quality products.

headline: 400 Southwest Wyoming Trona Mining Jobs On Hold As China Floods Soda Ash Market | Cowboy State Daily

Pacific Soda has been trying to build its Dry Creek expansion since 2019. While the Trump administration has improved some aspects of the permitting process the company faced under the Biden administration, the project still had to jump through many hoops. “You’ve got to do like archaeological clearances, cultural clearances. headline: White oil players in focus as Ukraine drone attacks hit Russia's Omsk refinery · Business Upturn
summary_text: # White oil stocks Gandhar Oil, Panama Petrochem in focus as ... strikes on Russian refineries tighten ... Shares of Indian white oil makers Gandhar Oil Refinery and Panama Petrochem are in focus as a wave of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries, including the Omsk refinery that processes white oil, raises the prospect of tighter global supply and firmer prices for the speciality product. Omsk is one of the larger refineries in the region, and its disruption has been accompanied by reports of fuel and petrochemical shortages within Russia. ... The backdrop is an intensifying campaign against Russia's oil infrastructure. According to a Meduza report drawing on a BBC Russian Service interview, an underground network called Chernaya Iskra, or Black Spark, says it has helped Ukraine strike nine refineries across Russia since September 2025, including the Omsk refinery, the country's largest by crude processing volume. The group, whose public face is former Gazprom executive Igor Volobuev, identifies critical and vulnerable sections of Russian refineries and passes that information to the Ukrainian military. The Omsk facility was hit in a drone attack in early July 2026. ... The relevance for Indian companies lies in the white oil supply chain. White oils are highly refined mineral oils used across pharmaceuticals, cosmetics, food processing and industrial applications, and disruption to a major processing hub such as Omsk can tighten global availability and lift prices for the product and its feedstock. For Indian white oil and speciality petroleum makers such as Gandhar Oil Refinery and Panama Petrochem, firmer international prices can support realisations, though the effect on margins depends on how their own input costs move at the same time. ... summary_text: Billionaire Christo Wiese’s Shoprite buys Africa’s largest coffee chain, Vida e Caffè, in $62 million deals after $16.8 billion annual sales | Business Insider Africa ... # Billionaire Christo Wiese’s Shoprite buys Africa’s largest coffee chain, Vida e Caffè, in $62 million deals after $16.8 billion annual sales Olamilekan Okebiorun 02 September 2026 10:53 AM South Africa’s Shoprite has agreed to acquire 100% of Vida e Caffè, Africa’s largest coffee chain, as the retailer broadens its business beyond supermarkets after posting R270.8 billion ($16.8 billion) in annual sales. ... - Shoprite has agreed to acquire 100% of Vida e Caffè, one of Africa’s largest coffee chains, as part of its strategy to expand beyond traditional grocery retail. - The deal covers Vida’s South African and international operations, pending regulatory approval, and is expected to become effective in the 2027 financial year. - Shoprite is also acquiring a majority stake in R&A Cellular, with both deals totaling about R1 billion ($62 million). - Vida e Caffè operates around 400 stores across several African countries and offers Shoprite access to more flexible, smaller retail formats including quick-service outlets. The August 20, 2026 agreement covers Vida’s South African and international operations and remains subject to regulatory approval, with completion expected in Shoprite’s 2027 financial year. Shoprite announced the acquisition alongside its annual results and another deal for a majority stake in payments company R&A Cellular. Together, the transactions are valued at about R1 billion ($62 million). Vida has grown from a single Cape Town café into about 400 corporate and franchise stores across Africa, making it the continent’s largest coffee chain and putting it ahead of regional rival Seattle Coffee Company, which operates roughly 300 outlets. Shoprite CEO Pieter Engelbrecht said Vida provides a strong platform for further growth. “Vida is a business we greatly admire, and we look forward to learning from its success while supporting its next phase of growth,” Engelbrecht said. The acquisition also gives Shoprite a direct foothold in the stand-alone quick-service restaurant market, where its exposure has largely been through in-store food and coffee operations. ... South African billionaire Christo Wiese remains influential at ... , with his stake in the retailer among his most valuable assets. Forbes estimates his fortune at about $1.9 billion, built largely through decades of investments in retail businesses including Pepkor and Shoprite. Although he stepped down as chairman in 2020, Wiese remains a non-executive director and chairs Shoprite’s Finance and Investment Committee, while Wendy Lucas-Bull chairs the board and Pieter Engelbrecht serves as CEO. The Vida deal comes as Shoprite continues to grow despite strategic exits from several African markets. Group sales rose 7.2% to R270.8 billion ($16.8 billion) in the 2026 financial year, while headline earnings per share increased 12.2%. That growth remains heavily concentrated in South Africa, where supermarket sales reached R228.7 billion ($14.2 billion), compared with R22.8 billion ($1.4 billion) from operations elsewhere on the continent. Outside South Africa, Shoprite’s supermarket business is now concentrated in Angola, Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Namibia, Zambia and Mozambique. Shoprite is also expanding into financial services through R&A Cellular, extending its reach into payments and informal retail. ... ## A different route into Africa The acquisitions come after years of scaling back the supermarket empire Shoprite built across Africa. headline: Shoprite orders the usual: a growthacino to go
summary_text: There is nothing skinny about Shoprite’s margins, and the lattes it’s about to bring in-house buy the retail juggernaut another growth option in its seemingly unstoppable conquest of the South African supermarket business ... A Vida e Cafe coffee. Picture supplied Grabbing a quick coffee is how you might describe one of Shoprite’s latest purchases. That’s because the nation’s largest retailer can pay for Vida e Caffe, the lively red chain of more than 400 coffee shops, with a morning’s takings at the till. The other of “the two small” deals, in CEO Pieter Engelbrecht’s telling, is R&A Cellular, a device rental and merchant platform which will form part of the group’s larger financial services ambitions. And with merchandise sales reaching nearly R271bn for the 52 weeks ending 28 June (a 7.2% jump on the previous year), what the retailer is paying seems like a drop in an Americano cup. ... But these are the big, small punts a business with seemingly unshakeable momentum can take. And Shoprite Holdings certainly has momentum — it has just clocked its 89th consecutive month of market share gains, Engelbrecht told investors. More importantly, the company has managed to widen its gross profit margin to 24.5%, from 24.3% a year ago, and its trading margin to 6%, from 5.9%. As Engelbrecht points out, both grew faster than sales. This, he says, “shows the margin was exceptionally well managed, and so were the costs — hence the 12.2% growth in diluted headline earnings.” The market initially loved the story, pushing Shoprite shares over 3% higher; the stock slipped back however to close only 1.2% up on Tuesday. ... Still, the sheer scale of its growth is undeniably impressive. Checkers was again a standout success, growing sales by 10% the past year, some five times faster than the rest of the South African market. Over the past decade the brand’s sales have rocketed from R37bn to R105bn. And its store footprint is now 662, which includes 342 supermarkets, 40 hypers, and 352 liquor stores. Another 26 grocery stores and 31 liquor outlets are set to open in the current year. The growth of delivery superstar Checkers Sixty60 “slowed” to 34.7%, but now accounts for sales of more than R25bn. That is up from, well, zero in just six years. Recipes by Jamie Oliver in your Sixty60 bag tell you that Checkers obviously targets a more well-to-do customer than the original Shoprite brand. Hooking more affluent consumers has surely given profit margins a boost. And Engelbrecht’s team has cleverly done this by developing more than 600 premium private label products. Just think of the Forage Feast series endorsed by Michelin star chef Jan Hendrik van der Westhuizen. ... But Engelbrecht sees the caffeine fix as having an even wider appeal. He is keen to consolidate the group’s coffee holdings under Vida and use it as an opportunity for franchise-holders – that means OK Foods – to capture more value. This promises plenty of crimson takeaway cups in shoppers’ hands. But the other red brand in the stable, compared to competitors at least, can hardly be called a drag on the group. The Shoprite segment, which includes not only the no-frills stores of the same name, but also Shoprite Liquor, Shoprite Sixty60, Shoprite Cash and Carry, and USave, increased sales by a more modest 4.3% to almost R122bn. This, however, is no mean feat as the group experienced overall price deflation in this segment. That, of course, means only one thing. To grow sales, Shoprite needed to grow volumes. And they did. ... The group managed to achieve superior volume growth to peers, Merchant West Investment portfolio manager Izak van Niekerk points out. “And this was with their selling price inflation tracking well below official/headline food price inflation.” ... Engelbrecht puts it down to years of refining the business’s data toolkit. “In 2017 we laid the platform, and then we started building tools on top of it – one of which is the price optimisation model, which uses artificial intelligence, among other things.” It helps the business with product selection and price points and it hones in on the right relationship between price point and volume, he adds. The brains in Brackenfell also have a model for price personalisation, which could offer specials at an individual level. Together these tech tools have helped boost sales even as price inflation hovers around a seven year low. “For example, if you discount a product by 20%, it doesn’t mean volume grows by 20% – it might be more, or it might be less,” says Engelbrecht. Either fascinating or scary, depending on the shade you display on the techno-optimism-pessimism spectrum. Van Niekerk, for one, finds it fascinating. “An interesting item they mentioned as the power of their data, is around the fuel price swings we have had this year, that they could calculate it down to what the effect would be by item and then make decisions around that,” says Van Niekerk. Out of Engelbrecht’s control, though, is administered prices — the likes of water, electricity, and property rates. When he started 30 years ago, these represented less than 1% of costs; now they are at 2.3%. “And for a retailer, that additional 1.5% or so is an enormous amount of money on a sales value of R270bn,” he points out. Enough to buy plenty of coffee chains.

headline: Moldretail Group buys Merci chain amid antitrust review
summary_text: # Moldretail Group Acquires the Merci Chain: Deal in Jeopardy Due to Antitrust Concerns The deal by Moldova’s largest grocery retailer to acquire the Merci chain has come under antitrust scrutiny. The main issue under investigation is the risk that the market’s largest player could strengthen its dominant position. Following the first phase of the review, Moldretail Group was unable to allay the regulator’s concerns regarding a potential restriction of competition both in the food retail sector and in the market for retail chain procurement. ... Today, Moldretail Group already owns the country’s largest retail chains—Linella, Fidesco, Bravo, Cip Market, Slavena Megamarket, Fourchette, Toto, as well as the Nuca coffee shops. By the end of 2025, the company had increased its revenue by 25%—from 11.6 billion to 14.5 billion lei—opened 75 new stores, and expanded its network to 320 retail locations nationwide. The group’s assets grew by nearly 1.3 billion lei over the year—to 4.8 billion lei—and its workforce exceeded 7,000 people. ... In terms of sales volume, Moldretail Group ranks first among the top five supermarket chains. It is more than twice as large as its closest competitor, Imensitate (which owns the Local, Bonus, Foxy, and Primul chains), whose revenue in 2025 amounted to 7.2 billion lei. The rest of the top five are Supermarket Nr. 1 (3.5 billion lei), Kaufland Moldova (3.4 billion lei), and Metro Cash & Carry Moldova (3.2 billion lei). Against this backdrop, Moldretail Grup, with nearly 16 billion lei in revenue, is the undisputed leader, while focusing on extensive growth. Last year alone, it opened nearly a hundred retail outlets across Moldova, and it doesn’t plan to stop there. ... Given this market consolidation, the regulator fears that the acquisition of Merci will further strengthen Moldretail Group’s position. The Competition Council points out that in certain regions of the country, the combined chain could gain a dominant position not only in retail trade but also in the procurement of food products for retail chains. ... Another risk relates to suppliers. According to the regulator’s assessment, some manufacturers that have worked with the Merci chain but do not do business with other Moldretail Group stores may lose their sales channels once the deal is finalized. This could increase suppliers’ dependence on the country’s largest retailer and reduce their bargaining power. ... At the same time, the Competition Council emphasizes that the launch of the second phase of the investigation does not imply a finding that the transaction is unlawful. An in-depth analysis is needed to assess all the consequences of the merger. In accordance with the law, Moldretail Group has the right to propose a set of commitments that would eliminate the identified competition risks and preserve the possibility of completing the transaction. ... It should be noted that the acquisition of Honest Company was announced in June 2026. It involves bringing the Merci chain of stores under the control of Moldretail Group through the acquisition of 100% of the company’s share capital. If the transaction is approved, Moldova’s largest grocery retailer will further strengthen its position in a market undergoing a period of rapid consolidation. In 2025 alone, 16 chains opened 220 new stores, compared to 142 the previous year. Moldretail Group and Imensitate accounted for about 60% of all new retail outlets in the country.

This move follows a turbulent period earlier this year when the discount grocer shuttered nine California stores, a decision that signaled a broader cooling of the company’s aggressive brick-and-mortar growth strategy. By anchoring its re-entry in the Inland Empire, the company is attempting to balance its operational footprint with the realities of a shifting consumer landscape. ... The closure of nine California stores earlier in 2026 was not merely a cost-cutting exercise; it was a corrective measure against the pressures of an inflationary market. Grocery Outlet, which relies heavily on an “opportunistic” buying model—purchasing overstock or close-dated goods from name-brand manufacturers—found itself navigating a complex supply chain environment where the availability of discounted inventory became increasingly inconsistent. ... According to official company disclosures, the decision to close those specific sites was driven by a rigorous evaluation of store-level profitability in regions where labor costs and overhead were outpacing the margins afforded by their low-price model. For a retailer that prides itself on being a “treasure hunt” for bargain shoppers, the math becomes precarious when fixed costs rise faster than the volume of discounted goods available to sell. ... The choice of Ontario Ranch for this new expansion is far from accidental. The Inland Empire remains one of California’s most resilient logistics and residential hubs. Unlike the saturated markets of coastal California, Ontario Ranch offers a growing demographic of value-conscious consumers who align perfectly with Grocery Outlet’s core value proposition. ... Industry analysts point out that the retailer is shifting from a “growth at all costs” mentality to a “targeted density” strategy. This approach focuses on regions where the company can leverage existing distribution channels while minimizing the logistical burden of servicing isolated, underperforming stores. By clustering locations, they reduce the per-unit cost of transportation and regional management. ... The broader retail climate in California remains fraught with challenges, from high utility costs to persistent wage inflation. Retail experts emphasize that the discount grocery segment is currently undergoing a structural transformation. As traditional supermarkets struggle to maintain price parity, chains like Grocery Outlet are positioning themselves as the primary alternative for households feeling the squeeze of the “cost-of-living” crisis. ... “The discount grocery sector is currently the only segment of the retail market seeing consistent, organic demand growth,” notes David Livingston, a veteran grocery industry consultant. “Retailers like Grocery Outlet aren’t just selling food; they are providing a necessary financial buffer for families. However, the operational challenge remains the same: scaling that model without losing the agility that makes the prices so low in the first place.” ... This sentiment is echoed by broader economic data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, which continues to track significant fluctuations in food-at-home price indices. For Grocery Outlet, the ability to pivot back to expansion suggests that they have successfully identified a supply-chain equilibrium that allows for profitable growth, even in a high-cost environment like California. ... While the Ontario Ranch opening is a positive signal for shareholders, it also underscores the fragility of the discount model. The company’s ability to thrive depends on its stock market performance and its success in maintaining relationships with major food suppliers who provide the inventory that drives their business. For the average shopper, this expansion means more than just a new store opening; it represents a test of whether the discount model can survive the permanent elevation of operating costs in the Golden State. As Grocery Outlet moves forward, the focus will likely remain on smaller, more efficient footprints rather than the expansive, high-rent locations of the past.

headline: International Workplace Group Adds New Regus In Stratford-Upon-Avon, As Demand For Flexible And Platform Working Continues To Accelerate

headline: IWG Accelerates Global Expansion with Record-Breaking 728 New Flexible Workspace Locations Signed in First Half of 2026
summary_text: August 28, 2026 International Workplace Group (IWG), a global leader in flexible workspace solutions and operator of prominent brands such as Regus and Spaces, has announced a significant acceleration in its expansion strategy. The company reported signing an impressive 728 new flexible workspace locations during the first half of 2026. This figure represents a substantial 47% increase compared to the 496 locations signed during the same period in the previous year, highlighting a robust demand for flexible working environments. In parallel, IWG also demonstrated strong operational growth by opening 425 new locations, a notable rise from the 338 opened in the first half of 2025. ... The company’s robust performance is further underscored by its financial results. For the first half of 2026, IWG’s revenue reached $2.4 billion, an 11% increase from the $2.2 billion recorded in the corresponding period of 2025. These interim results, released on August 11, 2026, reflect a sustained upward trajectory in the flexible workspace market, driven by evolving work preferences and corporate strategies. ... A key driver behind IWG’s rapid expansion is its strategic reliance on a capital-light managed partnership model. Approximately 95% of the new locations signed in the first half of 2026 were secured through this model. This approach allows IWG to expand its branded network significantly without incurring the substantial capital investment typically required for company-owned sites. By partnering with property owners and developers, IWG leverages existing real estate assets, reducing financial risk and accelerating market penetration. ... The success of this strategy is evident in the financial performance of its managed and franchised locations. Revenue generated from these partnerships saw a remarkable 36% year-over-year increase. Furthermore, recurring management fees, a crucial indicator of the growing scale and profitability of its partnership model, surged by an impressive 84% to reach $35 million. In contrast, revenue from company-owned locations also showed healthy growth, generating $1.865 billion, a 5% increase from $1.77 billion in the prior year. This dual-pronged financial growth strategy underscores IWG’s ability to scale effectively through both direct ownership and strategic partnerships. ... Further bolstering its network and strategic reach, IWG completed a significant acquisition in July 2026. The company acquired Wojo, a French flexible workspace operator, from its previous owners, Bouygues Immobilier and Accor. This acquisition not only added 186 established locations to IWG’s global portfolio but also solidified a long-term strategic relationship with Accor, a prominent global hospitality group. This partnership opens up potential avenues for IWG to integrate flexible workspace solutions within Accor’s extensive network of hotels, creating new opportunities for hybrid work models and business services. ... As of the end of the first half of 2026, IWG’s operational footprint was substantial, with 358,000 spaces already open globally. An additional 257,000 spaces were under contract and awaiting opening. Once these new locations are fully operational and mature, IWG projects they will contribute more than $2 billion in annual system-wide revenue. This pipeline of future growth signifies IWG’s continued commitment to expanding its global presence and meeting the escalating demand for flexible workspaces. The company’s total global network now surpasses 6,000 locations, a testament to its aggressive expansion and its dedication to bringing flexible workspace solutions to markets far beyond traditional central business districts. ... IWG, with its established brands and extensive global network, was well-positioned to capitalize on this trend. The company’s strategic decision to heavily invest in a capital-light partnership model has proven particularly astute. This approach allows for rapid scaling, enabling IWG to quickly establish a presence in new markets and meet the immediate demand without the significant financial burden of direct property acquisition and management. This is crucial in a real estate market that can be volatile and where upfront capital can be a barrier to entry. ... The acquisition of Wojo and the subsequent partnership with Accor represent a strategic move to diversify IWG’s offerings and tap into new customer segments. Integrating flexible workspace solutions into hotel infrastructure can cater to business travelers, remote workers seeking a temporary professional space, and companies looking for flexible meeting room solutions. This integration aligns with the growing trend of "work from anywhere" and the blurring lines between business and leisure travel. ... The projected revenue of over $2 billion from newly signed locations upon maturity signals strong future growth prospects for IWG. This indicates a confidence in the sustained demand for flexible workspaces and the ability of IWG’s model to generate significant revenue. The company’s ambition to reach over 6,000 locations globally demonstrates a clear strategy to dominate the flexible workspace market and provide a comprehensive solution for businesses of all sizes. ... However, this rapid expansion also presents challenges. Ensuring consistent quality across thousands of diverse locations, managing a complex network of partners, and adapting to the evolving needs of businesses will require robust operational management and continuous innovation. Furthermore, as the market matures, competition is likely to intensify, necessitating IWG to maintain its competitive edge through service excellence, technological integration, and a deep understanding of customer requirements.

headline: IWG 2026 Midyear Update: Record Results Meet A Historic Leadership Transition
summary_text: IWG plc, the Jersey-incorporated, Switzerland-domiciled owner of Regus, Spaces, HQ and Signature, enters mid-2026 in an unusual position: delivering its strongest-ever operating results just as it ends the nearly four-decade era of founder Mark Dixon as chief executive. ... IWG’s preliminary results for the year ended December 31, 2025, published on March 3, 2026, showed system-wide revenue of $4.5 billion and adjusted EBITDA of $531 million, its strongest operational year to date. Growth was modest at the group level — system-wide revenue rose 4% year-over-year, while adjusted EBITDA increased 6% from 2024 — but the composition of that growth is the real story. Adjusted gross profit increased 9% to over $1 billion, and the Company-owned segment margin rose to 26% from 25%. The standout was the Managed & Franchised division, IWG’s capital-light growth engine. System-wide revenue in that division increased 28%, with recurring management fees surging 140% to $45 million from $19 million in 2024. Recurring management fees are expected to reach $80 million in 2026 and $125 million in 2027, and the company has repeatedly compared its trajectory to established hotel franchisors such as Marriott and Hilton, noting it is still well below their typical proportion of fee-based revenue. ... Network expansion also hit records: 1,132 centers were signed (up 26%) and 782 centers opened (up 25%), giving IWG over 1 million rooms across 4,609 centers in more than 120 countries, with an additional 230,000 rooms in the pipeline. On the balance sheet, IWG continued a multi-year deleveraging effort. Net debt declined to $715 million from $729 million in 2024, improving the leverage ratio to 1.35x EBITDA from 1.45x. This came despite returning $144 million to shareholders through $130 million in buybacks and $14 million in dividends. Guidance for 2026 points to further progress, with adjusted EBITDA guidance set at $585 million to $625 million and a new $100 million buyback program announced for 2026, though the company has flagged that net debt is expected to rise slightly in 2026 even as capital returns continue. ... Despite the record headline figures, the market reaction was muted to negative: IWG’s stock declined 8.4% to £2.13 on the day of the results presentation. Analysts have pointed to structural concerns rather than execution — one summary noted the stock’s score is primarily constrained by high balance-sheet leverage, including negative equity, and a sharp 2025 deterioration in revenue, margins and cash flow versus 2024 on certain measures, even as the underlying franchise transition progresses. There is also a broader sector overhang: reports note the share price was negatively impacted by market concerns over AI, which affected perceptions of the commercial property sector, given fears that AI-driven productivity gains could eventually reduce corporate demand for physical office space — an irony given IWG’s own flexible-space model is often pitched as a hedge against exactly that uncertainty. ... On June 16, 2026, IWG announced a significant reshaping of its top leadership. Christian Schmitz was appointed Chief Executive Officer, with founder Mark Dixon transitioning to Executive Chair and Douglas Sutherland becoming Deputy Chair, moving up from his prior role as Non-Executive Chair. ... Dixon’s departure from the CEO role is historically significant. The transition sees Dixon hand over the reins to insider Christian Schmitz after nearly 40 years in the role, having founded IWG in 1989 and built a network spanning more than 120 countries through brands such as Regus, Spaces, HQ and Signature. In the company’s own words, Dixon reflected that it had been a privilege to lead the company as it grew to 6,000 locations open and in the pipeline worldwide since founding it with a single Brussels center. ... Schmitz is very much an internal appointment rather than an outside hire, which the company has framed as ensuring continuity. ... joined IWG last year as chief transformation officer before being promoted to ... , and brings ... background as a partner at McKinsey, a director at KKR Capstone, and previously CEO of Selecta for six years. Dixon has publicly endorsed the choice, saying Schmitz has made a significant impact, bringing deep insight into our business and a clear focus on execution, and ... well placed to lead the company’s next growth phase. ... Reuters framed the reshuffle in blunter commercial terms, reporting the changes come as the company seeks to cut debt and costs amid geopolitical and AI-driven pressures, and that IWG has been tackling rising debt and costs, pressured by the fallout of the Middle East conflict and AI-driven shifts in workplace strategy. That framing sits somewhat in tension with the company’s own “record results” narrative, and underscores that the succession, while presented as proactive and orderly, is also occurring against a backdrop of real financial and macro pressure. ... Taken together, the results and the succession tell a coherent story about an inflection point rather than a crisis. IWG’s underlying operating metrics — network growth, fee income, EBITDA, deleveraging — are moving in the right direction, and the shift toward a franchise-heavy, capital-light model mirrors a well-trodden playbook from the hotel industry. At the same time, elevated leverage, a still-large net debt position, and investor anxiety about AI’s long-term effect on office demand mean the market has not fully rewarded that operational progress. ... Handing day-to-day execution to an internal transformation specialist, while keeping the founder engaged as an adviser and the company’s largest shareholder, is a low-disruption way to test whether professional management can accelerate the deleveraging and franchise-fee growth story without losing strategic continuity. Whether investors come to see this as effective succession planning or as evidence of deeper pressure on the business will likely depend on how quickly Schmitz can translate record operating metrics into a re-rating of the stock, and on whether net debt reduction resumes in 2026 despite the guided uptick.

MOORESTOWN, NJ, UNITED STATES, August 6, 2026 / EINPresswire.com/ -- Nectar, an independent retail media and commerce agency and Amazon Ads Advanced Partner, today introduced Nectar Cue, an AI workflow platform for Amazon and marketplace brands. Cue is built on two systems Nectar already operates: iDerive, its proprietary commerce analytics platform, and the iDerive MCP server, which connects that data securely to AI assistants including Claude. Together they let a brand ask a question about its entire Amazon business in plain language and get an answer the same day. The same analysis has historically taken an analyst most of a week. Most brands can build a custom audience in Amazon Marketing Cloud. Most never act on it. Audiences built in AMC, Amazon’s clean-room analytics environment — lapsed Subscribe & Save customers, competitor-cart shoppers, high-LTV lookalikes, true new-to-brand segments with five-year suppression logic — only matter if their impact can be measured. iDerive unifies AMC audience and measurement data with sales, advertising, and profitability down to the SKU and search-term level, so every question about growth is answered against profit. That measurement layer is what Cue runs on. Access runs through the iDerive MCP server, built on Model Context Protocol, the open standard introduced by Anthropic for connecting AI assistants to live data. Brands query their own marketplace data from their own Claude account, with no analyst in the loop. A brand manager can ask which new-to-brand segments are growing, how they overlap with current spend, and where the next dollar earns the most margin, and see the answer in seconds instead of waiting for a report to be assembled. The insight does not stop at analysis. Nectar’s advertising teams take the same audience logic into Amazon DSP, Amazon’s programmatic ad platform, and into audience-based bid modifiers on Sponsored Products and Sponsored Brands, reaching the shoppers search alone cannot: competitor buyers, lapsed customers, and category newcomers. iDerive then measures whether that activation was incremental, in new-to-brand rate and contribution margin rather than ROAS alone. Cue extends the same foundation from answering questions to running the work. Reaching Amazon Marketing Cloud, Vendor and Seller Central, Amazon Ads, and additional marketplaces through one connection, Cue turns recurring analysis into monitored workflows. It surfaces exceptions, such as a suppressed listing or an emerging revenue opportunity, and routes them to the person who can act. For brands running thousands of SKUs, the binding constraint is rarely analysis; it is the hours available to catch and act on what the analysis finds. Cue is in use across Nectar’s own analyst teams today and is rolling out to brand partners in phases. “AMC changed the question from where should we bid to who are we bidding on,” said Harriet Carson, VP of Advertising at Nectar. “Nectar Cue lets us answer that question in plain language and act on it the same day. We take the audiences we build straight into the DSP and Sponsored Ads campaigns our team runs, and we can prove in dollars whether they were incremental.” The approach is already producing results for Nectar’s partners. Petmate grew new-to-brand orders by about 85 percent and Core ASIN revenue by 12 percent through audience-led advertising measured in iDerive. Boxie increased ordered revenue on Amazon Canada by 55.4 percent on roughly half a percent more ad spend. Epson lifted ad-attributed sales 153 percent while keeping ad spend steady. “A custom audience is only as valuable as your ability to prove it moved the business,” said Youval Peltier, Chief Strategy Officer at Nectar. “Nectar Cue gives our team and our clients the same answer, in dollars, the same day. Connecting iDerive to Claude means a brand can ask its own data a question and see where the profitable growth is, without waiting for a report.” The iDerive MCP server is available to iDerive clients today, and brands can connect iDerive to Claude as part of their engagement. Nectar Cue is rolling out in phases, beginning with Nectar’s team and select brand partners. An Amazon Ads Advanced Partner and Walmart Connect Partner Network member, Nectar combines an in-house creative studio, marketplace advertising across Sponsored Ads, DSP, and AMC, 1P and 3P operations, and its proprietary iDerive analytics platform. headline: Dominion and NextEra File Joint Petition for Virginia SCC Approval of Merger | Williams Mullen
summary_text: Dominion and NextEra File Joint Petition for Virginia SCC Approval of Merger | Williams Mullen 07.17.2026 Legal News # Dominion and NextEra File Joint Petition for Virginia SCC Approval of Merger By: Bradley J. Nowak Summary — Dominion Energy and NextEra Energy have formally initiated Virginia's review of their proposed merger by seeking State Corporation Commission approval for NextEra's acquisition of indirect control of Dominion Energy Virginia. The filing marks a key milestone in the broader regulatory approval process, with the companies proposing a range of customer and operational commitments as they pursue a target closing in the second half of 2027. ... On July 15, 2026, Dominion Energy, Inc., Virginia Electric and Power Company (Dominion Energy Virginia), NextEra Energy, Inc., and related entities filed a Joint Petition (the “Joint Petition”) with the Virginia State Corporation Commission (the “Commission”) seeking approval under Virginia’s Utility Transfers Act for NextEra’s acquisition of indirect control of Dominion Energy Virginia through the companies’ proposed holding company merger. The filing formally commences the Virginia regulatory review process for one of the transaction’s principal state approvals. ... The Joint Petition follows the parties’ execution of an Agreement and Plan of Merger on May 15, 2026. Under the proposed transaction, NextEra would acquire Dominion through a two-step holding company merger, with Dominion Energy Virginia remaining a separately incorporated Virginia public utility operating under its existing name, service territory, and regulatory framework. The filing states that the parties currently expect the transaction to close during the second half of 2027, subject to receipt of all required regulatory approvals and satisfaction of other closing conditions. ... The petition seeks approval under Chapter 5 of Title 56 of the Virginia Code (the “Transfers Act”) because the transaction results in an indirect transfer of control of Dominion Energy Virginia. Although the Joint Petition indicates that no utility assets are being transferred and no changes to existing rates or service are proposed, Commission approval is required before the change in control can occur. The petition also requests confirmation that any approval extends to OSW Project LLC, a Dominion affiliate that owns the Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind (CVOW) project. ... ’s Transfers Act ... an expedited review schedule once ... Commission determines that ... - July 15, 2026 – Joint Petition filed with the Commission. - Within 60 days of filing a complete application – The Commission must approve or deny the petition unless it extends the review period. - Up to an additional 120 days – The Commission may extend the statutory review period by order. - If the Commission does not act within the statutory period – The application is deemed approved by operation of law. - Second half of 2027 – Anticipated closing of the merger, assuming receipt of all required regulatory approvals and satisfaction of closing conditions. ... To support approval under the Transfers Act, in the Joint Petition, Dominion and NextEra propose a package of voluntary commitments, including: ... - Approximately $2.25 billion in shareholder-funded customer bill credits for Dominion customers across Virginia, North Carolina, and South Carolina, with approximately $1.78 billion (approximately 79%) allocated to Virginia customers over a 24-month period following closing. Credits are designed to provide a typical residential customer using 1,000 kWh per month with a $10 monthly bill credit; ... - A commitment that customers will bear no merger-related costs, including transaction expenses, financing costs, acquisition premiums, restructuring costs, or transition costs; ... - Establishment of Richmond, Virginia, as a dual corporate headquarters alongside Juno Beach, Florida; ... - Continuation of Dominion Energy Virginia’s existing management team, including Edward H. Baine as President; ... - Commitments to maintain separate books and records, preserve strong investment-grade credit metrics, and maintain local operational decision-making; ... - Commitment by NextEra to provide equity financing, as needed, to Dominion Energy Virginia to maintain its capital structure and credit metrics; ... - Employee protections, including 18 months of job protection following closing and two years of compensation and benefits protection for non-union employees; and ... - An additional $10 million annually in shareholder-funded charitable contributions for at least five years following closing, allocated among Virginia, North Carolina, and South Carolina consistent with historical average giving levels. ... Further, with respect to the Virginia Clean Economy Act, in testimony submitted by Edward Baine, President of Dominion Energy Virginia, he states that “[Dominion Energy Virginia] will remain fully dedicated to the nation-leading public policy priorities that Virginia has established, including through the Virginia Clean Economy Act (‘VCEA’), with its reliability backstop, and related commitments and targets in other legislation.” ... The filing notes that the merger also requires additional approvals and other closing conditions, including: ... - the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission; - the Nuclear Regulatory Commission; - the North Carolina Utilities Commission; - the South Carolina Public Service Commission; - expiration or termination of the applicable waiting period under the Hart-Scott-Rodino Antitrust Improvements Act of 1976; and - shareholders of both Dominion and NextEra. ... The July 15 filing marks the formal beginning of Virginia’s review of the proposed Dominion–NextEra transaction. While the Transfers Act provides for an expedited statutory review period, with a 60-day initial deadline that may be extended by up to an additional 120 days, the overall merger remains subject to multiple state and federal approvals before the parties’ anticipated closing in the second half of 2027. Through a package of proposed conditions, including customer bill credits, governance commitments, operational protections, and customer safeguards, the applicants seek to demonstrate that the transaction satisfies Virginia’s statutory standard that adequate service at just and reasonable rates will not be impaired.

Victoria Higgins, director of Chesapeake Climate Action Network Virginia, said the merger is about seizing control of Virginia's " Data Center Alley," arguing that smaller ratepayers face disproportionate costs in serving demand brought about by the state's biggest energy users. ... "Already, Virginians are being asked to bankroll the wealthiest companies in the world," Higgins wrote. US utilities NextEra Energy and Dominion Energy have formally submitted applications to state and federal governments to merge their companies, creating the largest regulated power utility in the world. ... The companies submitted applications to the Virginia State Corporation Commission, the North Carolina Utilities Commission, the Public Service Commission of South Carolina, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, seeking regulatory approval of their merger. ... If approved, the new company would serve around 10 million customers across Virginia, the Carolinas and Florida, making it the largest single regulated power utility on earth and the largest overall power company in the US. The transaction is expected to close in the second half of 2027. ... The companies claim that the merger would “preserve Dominion Energy’s local strengths with NextEra Energy’s added resources, balance sheet strength, supply chain expertise, construction experience and operating capabilities”, and that it would be “better positioned to buy, build, finance and operate the energy infrastructure customers need more efficiently.” ... It positioned the move around the “rapidly growing electricity demand” in the US, largely from data centres, and the expansions in both power generation and grid infrastructure that growth will require. ... John Ketchum, chairman, president and CEO of NextEra Energy, said: “This combination is about putting scale and a stronger, more comprehensive platform behind Dominion Energy’s local teams so they can meet growing power demand while keeping bills affordable and service reliable. ... “Together, we will be better positioned to partner with states and communities to attract new investment, support new jobs and invest in the all-of-the-above energy infrastructure customers need, including renewables, battery storage, nuclear and gas-fired generation. Customers would experience immediate value through $2.25 billion in shareholder-funded bill credits and long-term value through a stronger company that can buy, build, finance and operate energy infrastructure projects more efficiently, which will result in long-term customer benefits.” ... However, various groups in the US have urged caution over the merger, its potential impact on consumers in the relevant states and the massive power that a utility of that size would wield. ... Groups including Secure Solar Futures, Public Citizen and Clean Virginia warned back in May that it could be “very challenging to counter the political influence” of the new entity, which would have more than five times the current net worth of Dominion Energy. They also warned that if the new entity focuses on large, costly, centralised infrastructure development it could ultimately raise rates for consumers. The growth of data centres, which is already impacting Virginia, in particular, will “likely” increase energy prices for users, according to a report by the Virginia Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission (JLARC). ... The groups said that amid this transformation of US power demand, regulators should ensure that the birth of a company as unprecedentedly large as the NextEra-Dominion merger prioritises modernisation, distributed energy sources and “builds an energy system designed not simply to expand, but to optimise, adapt, and evolve for the decades ahead.”
